column13:
The Beautiful Game presents a playable selection of soccer video games spanning the last 50 years. The exhibit traces how the world’s most popular sport has been imagined for players on screen, from early home console experiments to influential titles that helped define modern sports gaming. It invites visitors to celebrate soccer’s global history through play as the beautiful game comes home to Toronto.

Beginning with early interpretations on platforms such as the Atari 2600, where soccer was represented through simple graphics and fast reflexes, the exhibition follows the sport’s digital evolution through home consoles like the Nintendo Entertainment System and into the rise of landmark franchises such as FIFA International Soccer. Displayed side by side, these games reveal how advances in technology reshaped ideas of realism, competition, and spectacle across generations.

This exhibit is a collaboration between the Royal Ontario Museum, the University of Toronto Mississauga Library with its extensive Syd Bolton Collection of video games, and the Broken Games Collective, a community of practice that champions restoring access to games that are broken, obsolete, or inaccessible. Together, they bring historical hardware, software, and curatorial expertise into a shared space that recognizes retro video games as cultural artifacts, preserving how generations of players have engaged with soccer beyond the stadium and onto the screen.

Award-winning game developer Tanya Kan brings her 14 years of industry experience to help you prioritize and augment your creative power, emphasizing human-first artistry and problem-solving. Let’s celebrate making the creative media that drives you!

There are so many moving parts to bringing a creative project to life. For example, from ideation to launch, a video game can have immense scope, creative, technical, administrative, and psychological challenges. Whether you are working on a 3-month long Youtube project, a 6-month long interior design project, or a 4-year long game project, let’s journal together to frame our goals, priorities, and plans wisely. Bring your favorite journals and writing tools. All experience levels, solo or teams, and disciplines are welcome!

This Cozy Journalling session will have some big changes from last year’s session: There will be an all-new production management for teams module section inspired by Kim Scott’s book “Radical Respect”, more design thinking aimed at early professionals, and more opportunity for participants to reframe their energy about their creative strengths. I will also save more time for these topics by not discussing fountain pens, as I think that falls outside the 1.5 to 2 hour time limits.

Baby Ghosts runs a program called Cooperative Foundations that helps indie game studios learn cooperative governance and build sustainable studio structures. We're currently working with 10+ Toronto-based studios at various stages.

This event would be a facilitated roundtable conversation with members of these studios, talking honestly about what it's like to try to build a cooperative game studio, the challenges, the things that are working, and what they're figuring out as they go. We're aiming for real conversation between the devs, not a panel where everyone presents one by one. Audience participation and questions will be taken throughout.

We're planning for 50-100 people. We'd have a facilitator from our team running the conversation, and we're hoping to show some gameplay on a shared screen during the social period after. Studios we're hoping to feature include Rocket Adrift, Amelore, Doomscroll Studios, See in Red, Polyvale Studios, Covert Sky, and three studios from our current cohort.

column12: In this cognitive imagination workshop, literally and figuratively map your internal world, crafting abstracted artifacts generated through a poetic reimagining of psychological profiling and journaling keepsake games. Materials provided, though you may bring your own journal or sketchbook. Part of the “Play Outside the Box” event series.
column13:
itch.io page: https://gblekkenhorst.itch.io/nonsensitive 
Few people spend much time thinking about HOW they think - our thoughts and memories can form in the language of our culture, the language of our senses, sometimes in a language that can only exist within us. How clear and detailed our thoughts are, and which imaginative medium we reach for while we're trying to form them, are highly individual and often invisible to us.

Do you have an interior monologue? Can you form a picture in your mind? Maybe a smell reminds you of something - but can you remember a smell, or just the description of it? These languages might have a hard ceiling due to biological variance, but they are also a skill you can hone when you know what to reach for, like an artist learning how to see before putting pencil to page, or returning to the body during meditation.

Workshop participants craft artifacts that detail their cognitive imaginations that are deliberately enigmatic - sense becoming nonsense - inviting memory to devour the context of the experience, leaving physical evidence of the players tactile experience of inscribing it. Attendees are encouraged to bring their artifacts home to revisit the physical memory and see what they can piece back together, and to submit digitizations of their artifacts back to the project for future iterations.

The experience is part typographic poetry, part journaling keepsake game, and likely to generate discussions about what we learn about ourselves. The mapping itself gives insight into how we think, just by being asked a question about something we assumed was a given - but it's hearing how it's different for someone else that really illuminates how we work, and how we can empathize with different minds. (Remember this the next time someone doesn't notice your haircut.)

Materials will be provided, however attendees can bring their own journals or sketchbooks.
Part of the “Play Outside the Box” event series.

column3: Fight and Ye Shall Receive: How Game Worker Unions Win!
column11: Academics, Community, Industry, Game Creators
column12: Game workers from across the continent will discuss the historic rise of the game industry labour movement, how unions are making changes in our industry, and visions for the future! If you've  wondered how unionization could change your workplace and our whole industry, this talk is for you! A Q&A session and mixer with snacks will follow!
column13:
Game workers will discuss the historic rise of the game industry labour movement, how unions are making positive changes in our industry, and visions for the future!

Over the last few years, thousands of game workers across Canada and the US have won certified unions and bargained first contracts at major game studios like Bethesda, Blizzard, SEGA, Paizo, and more. 

Last year, the industry also saw the launch of United Videogame Workers (CWA Local 9433), a direct-to-join union established with CWA open to any game worker in North America.

If you've ever wondered about the specifics of how unionization could change or benefit your workplace and our whole industry, this talk is for you!

A moderated audience Q&A session and mixer will follow! Snacks provided!

---

The event will be a panel and mixer for games workers interested in unionization. The panel will consist of 3 or 4 workers involved in organizing efforts in the industry, and will be moderated by a CWA organizer. 

The panel will cover how panelists first got involved in organizing, what motivated them to start campaigns in their workplaces, and the shifts they’ve seen over the course of organizing. We’ll discuss the changes that panelists hope to see won through organizing, as well as how to overcome fears that workers can have about joining a union. We will also cover topics like the difference between traditional organizing campaigns, and a direct-join model exemplified by UVW.

Following the panel we plan to open up the conversation for audience Q&A, and let attendees ask questions about organizing based on their own experience. 

Before and after the panel we plan to open the space up for a mixer, to let attendees socialize and also have the opportunity to speak directly with organizers present as well as panelists. We plan to provide food during the mixer. In addition to panelists and our moderator, we’ll have other volunteers available to talk with attendees, as well as free zines and merch to take.

column12: What if a whole room could heal together? Flowr Choir brings families, kids, and curious humans of all ages into a shared somatic experience — phones in hand, voices raised, growing a living digital garden through breath and sound. It’s part concert, part science, part magic.
column13:
Your voice is alive!

FLOWR Choir is a drop-in, participatory live event where families, kids, and curious humans of all ages come together to grow a shared digital garden — using nothing but their voices, breath, and presence. Powered by FLOWR’s proprietary Sounding Core technology, participants’ vocal features are analyzed in real time, on-device, translating the acoustic qualities of breath and sound into a living, blooming visual world on screen.

This is not a passive demo. It’s a collective act of creation.

How It Works
Participants are onboarded onto FLOWR — loaded onto iPhones or provided devices — and guided into a simple, intuitive experience: hum, exhale, tone, sing. The game responds. Flowers grow. The garden changes. When many voices sound together, something larger emerges — a shared ecosystem that no single participant could have built alone. The experience is designed to be immediately accessible to a six-year-old and genuinely moving for an adult.
Underneath the magic is science. FLOWR’s Sounding Core uses an on-device GRU-CNN architecture to analyze vocal biomarkers associated with autonomic nervous system regulation. Toning and intentional vocalization are established mechanisms for stimulating the vagus nerve — the body’s primary parasympathetic pathway. FLOWR Choir is, quietly, a public health intervention dressed as a game.
column14: It’s a game where your voice grows flowers — and it’s physiologically calming your nervous system while you play.

Participating studios will be paying a $100 hanging fee to cover printing and framing for the main posters and they may also be able to submit additional frames work at no additional cost pending wall space.

Current Studio participating are BancyCo, Cococucumber, Numizmatic, Soft Rains, Alientrap, Kitten Cup, Hilltop Studios, and Mighty Yell

- Get a peek into the technical side with Ryan Miller—showing how we manage scaling Jinja’s Garden across a decade of hardware.

After the talks, we’re assembling some of the creative brains behind Jinja’s Garden for a Panel Discussion, moderated by our in-house animation genius, Yuliya Boublikova. You won’t want to miss hearing from these awesome folks:

- Tobias Bauer, Production Manager
- Nehir Dogan, 3D Artist
- Richard Hilmer, Lead Unity Developer
- Nik Aggarwal, Senior Game Developer
- Bryan Winters, Senior Game Developer
- David Czarnowski, Play Designer & Technical Artist

column13:
With further attacks on the rights of marginalized people comes an increased need for resistance. Continuing with our mission to give diverse game developers a space to share their work and build community, we are delighted to return for a second year!

DEI (Diversity, Equality, and Inclusion) efforts are still being targeted by right-wing governments in the US, Canada, and around the world. With an increased pressure on Trans people in particular and a continuing layoff crisis in the games industry has led many to consider quitting the business altogether.

The games industry is famously toxic and can be an extremely difficult place for developers from marginalized backgrounds to thrive. How can we challenge the narrative around DEI and push back against attacks on diversity in our industry? Our event will help participants understand the unique challenges marginalized people face - and that our choices often feel like "DEI or DIE".

column3: Drawing from Within: Create Your Own Personal Oracle Cards
column11: Academics, Community, Game Enthusiasts
column12: Explore your intuition through creative play! In this interactive workshop, you’ll craft a personalized oracle card using imagery and symbols that resonate with you. Then, enjoy a group reading where participants share and interpret each card’s story. All materials provided. All levels welcome.
column13:
This interactive workshop invites participants into the creative, playful, and reflective process of designing their own personalized oracle cards. Blending art-making with intuitive exploration and gentle art therapy practices, the session will create a welcoming space to reconnect with inner wisdom while engaging in a shared creative experience.

The workshop will begin with a brief, accessible introduction to symbolism in oracle and tarot traditions, including a light exploration of archetypes and the Major Arcana as representations of universal human experiences. Participants will be encouraged to reflect on how these symbolic frameworks mirror patterns, emotions, and parts within their own lives. This grounding offers a starting point for understanding how imagery and metaphor can act as powerful tools for self-reflection.

Participants will then be guided into creating their own cards using personally meaningful symbols, imagery, and themes. Through prompts, attendees will explore their inner landscape and translate their insights into visual form. The emphasis is on developing a personal symbolic language that feels authentic and resonant.

No prior experience with tarot, oracle cards, art, or parts work is required. All levels of familiarity are not only welcomed but valued, as the practice prioritizes process over final product, and curiosity and play over perfection. 

All art materials will be provided. Optional sharing throughout will support connection among attendees, fostering a sense of community in a relaxed, non-judgemental and supportive atmosphere.

The workshop will conclude with a collaborative group reading using the newly created deck. Participants will be invited to collectively draw and interpret cards, reflecting on how the imagery resonates with their own experiences. Each person will also have the opportunity to share the meaning behind their own card, offering insight into their chosen symbolism and the personal narratives or parts it represents. This closing practice will deepen both individual reflection and group connection, highlighting the richness of diverse perspectives and intuitive interpretation.

Led by: Athanasia Pallas, a Toronto based artist and writer, whose work draws on psychology, the esoteric and self-exploration. She is currently crafting an oracle deck to guide healing, inner parts work, and intuitive connection.

Co-hosted by: Droqen (Alexander Clair Tseu Martin), a lost game designer and abstract pixel artist, recently pursuing an interest in art therapy. Creator and reader of ‘Droqen’s Tarot’, a personal pixel art tarot deck inspired by game design.
column14: Explore your intuition through creative play by crafting a personalized oracle card and sharing its story in a lively, supportive group reading—no experience needed, all materials provided.
